blocks.content: There are two ways to design in an LLD interview: sketch the structure first as a diagram, or start writing classes directly. Both work, and neither is right or wrong. The real skill is knowing when to use each.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974121956-997437586.png

UML first means drawing the classes and their relationships before coding. Code first means jumping into writing class skeletons and letting the structure emerge. They suit different people and different problems.
This lesson explains both approaches in depth, weighs their tradeoffs, and gives you a practical middle path that most strong candidates actually use.

blocks.title: The honest truth
blocks.content: Interviewers do not care which one you pick. They care that your design is clear and that you can implement it. Choose whatever helps you communicate best.
1. What Each Approach Means
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972241263-782636753.png
blocks.alt: UML first draws before coding, code first lets structure emerge

blocks.content: UML first
You draw boxes for classes, list their fields and methods, and connect them with lines showing relationships. Only after the picture is clear do you write any code.
Code first
You start writing class skeletons straight away, adding fields and methods as you think, and let the design take shape on the page as you go.
Both aim at the same goal, a clean set of classes, they just arrive there from different directions.
A Quick Word on What UML Is
blocks.text: A Quick Word on What UML Is

blocks.content: UML, the Unified Modeling Language, is a standard way to draw software designs. For LLD, you only need the class diagram, which shows classes as boxes and relationships as lines.

["A box has three parts: the name, the fields, and the methods.","Lines connect classes to show associations and has a relationships.","A hollow arrow points from a child to its parent for inheritance."]
items: A box has three parts: the name, the fields, and the methods.
Lines connect classes to show associations and has a relationships.
A hollow arrow points from a child to its parent for inheritance.

blocks.title: You do not need perfect UML
blocks.content: A simple box and arrow sketch is enough in an interview. Precise notation is not the point, clear communication is.
2. A Simple Class Sketch
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974129057-311985486.png
blocks.alt: A simple parking lot class sketch

blocks.content: Here is what a rough class sketch captures, written out as the classes it represents.
That tiny map shows the fields, the key methods, and the relationships. Whether you draw it or write it, this is the structure you are agreeing on before coding.
UML First: How It Works
You spend the first part of the design drawing the class map. You place the entities, add their fields and methods, and connect them. Only once the picture makes sense do you turn boxes into code.
This suits complex problems with many classes, where seeing the whole shape first prevents you from getting lost in details.
3. UML First: The Tradeoffs

{"pros":["Gives a clear big picture before details","Makes relationships easy to see and discuss","Great for complex systems with many classes","Easy for the interviewer to follow along"],"cons":["Can eat time if you over polish the diagram","Risk of a pretty picture with no working code","Feels slow for simple problems"]}
Code First: How It Works
You start writing class skeletons immediately. As you add fields and methods, the relationships reveal themselves, and you adjust as you go.
This suits people who think in code and problems that are small and focused, where a full diagram would be overkill.
4. Code First: The Tradeoffs

{"pros":["Produces real, concrete classes quickly","Feels natural if you think in code","Shows you can actually implement, not just draw"],"cons":["Easy to lose the big picture","Relationships can get tangled without a map","Harder for the interviewer to see the whole design"]}
When to Use Which
Match the approach to the problem and to how you think best.

{"headers":["Situation","Better Approach"],"rows":[["Many entities and relationships","UML first, to map it out"],["A small, focused problem","Code first, to move fast"],["You think visually","UML first"],["You think in code","Code first"],["Complex inheritance to reason about","UML first"]]}
5. The Hybrid Approach
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972244514-123819731.png
You do not have to pick one purely. The approach many senior engineers use blends both, and it is the one we recommend.

["Sketch the key classes and their relationships quickly, with no attempt at perfection.","Confirm the structure with the interviewer out loud.","Then write the important classes and methods in code.","Refer back to the sketch as you extend the design during follow ups."]
items: Sketch the key classes and their relationships quickly, with no attempt at perfection.
Confirm the structure with the interviewer out loud.
Then write the important classes and methods in code.
Refer back to the sketch as you extend the design during follow ups.

blocks.content: A rough sketch plus real code beats a beautiful diagram with no implementation, every single time.
Reading Relationships in a Sketch
When you draw, a few simple conventions help the interviewer follow along without formal notation.
["A plain line for association, where one class uses another.","A line noting one or many for has a relationships.","An arrow toward the parent for inheritance, the is a relationship."]
items: A plain line for association, where one class uses another.
A line noting one or many for has a relationships.
An arrow toward the parent for inheritance, the is a relationship.

blocks.content: Clear, consistent arrows matter far more than exact UML symbols. The goal is shared understanding, not a textbook diagram.
6. A Worked Example, Both Ways
Take a small prompt, design a deck of cards, and see both approaches.
UML first
You would draw three boxes: Card with a suit and a rank, Deck holding a list of Cards, and an enum for Suit. Lines show the Deck has many Cards. Then you code from that map.
Code first
For a problem this small, code first is faster. For a full casino system with players, bets, and rules, sketching first would keep you oriented.
7. Communicate Whichever You Choose
The approach matters less than the talking. Whether you draw or code, narrate what each class is for and how it connects. A silent design is hard to follow no matter the method.

blocks.title: The real deciding factor
blocks.content: The interviewer wants to see both your structure and that you can implement it. Do not spend the whole session drawing, and do not code so fast the design becomes a tangle.
8. The Interview Reality

In practice, most successful candidates do a light hybrid: a two minute rough sketch to agree the shape, then straight into code. This gives the interviewer the map and gives you a finished, working design.
Time is the constraint. Whatever you choose, leave enough of the session to write the core classes, because a working design speaks louder than a drawing.
9. The Elements of a Class Box
blocks.text: 9. The Elements of a Class Box

blocks.content: A class in a sketch is a box with three parts stacked vertically: the class name on top, the fields in the middle, and the methods at the bottom.
A plus sign means public, a minus sign means private. That is nearly all the notation you need for an LLD sketch.
10. Showing Multiplicity in a Sketch
Next to a relationship line, a small label shows how many. A one and a star (meaning many) is the most common pair you will draw.
["1 to 1: a Ticket to one Vehicle","1 to many: a ParkingLot to many Levels","many to many: Students to Courses"]
items: 1 to 1: a Ticket to one Vehicle
1 to many: a ParkingLot to many Levels
many to many: Students to Courses

blocks.content: Marking one or many on the line tells the reader instantly whether a class holds a single reference or a list.
11. A Second Example: Chess, Both Ways
blocks.text: 11. A Second Example: Chess, Both Ways

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974131413-277371915.png
blocks.alt: A chess class sketch with piece inheritance

blocks.content: Take a chess game to see the two approaches once more.

blocks.title: UML first
blocks.text: Boxes for Board, Piece, and Player, with Piece as a parent of Pawn, Rook, and so on. Lines show a Board has many Pieces. Then you code from the map.

blocks.content: Chess has real inheritance among pieces, so a quick sketch of that hierarchy first keeps you oriented before you code.
12. Tips for a Clean Sketch
A few habits keep a sketch readable under interview pressure.

["Write only the important fields and methods, not every getter","Space boxes out so lines do not cross in a tangle","Use consistent arrows for the same kind of relationship","Leave room to add classes when follow ups arrive"]
items: Write only the important fields and methods, not every getter
Space boxes out so lines do not cross in a tangle
Use consistent arrows for the same kind of relationship
Leave room to add classes when follow ups arrive

blocks.content: 13. Practising Both Approaches

You do not have to commit to one style forever. Practise a few problems drawing a quick sketch first, and a few writing code straight away. You will soon feel which one suits you and which suits each kind of problem.
["Try a small problem code first, like a deck of cards","Try a large one sketch first, like a booking system","Notice where each felt faster and clearer"]
items: Try a small problem code first, like a deck of cards
Try a large one sketch first, like a booking system
Notice where each felt faster and clearer

blocks.title: Build your own instinct
blocks.content: After a handful of practice problems, choosing an approach becomes automatic. You will glance at a prompt and simply know whether to sketch or to code.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Sketch just enough to agree the shape","Move to code with time to spare","Explain your classes as you go","Pick the approach that fits the problem"],"cons":["Polishing a diagram for twenty minutes","Coding so fast it becomes a tangle","Designing in silence","Forcing UML on a tiny problem"]}
15. Common Questions
Which one do interviewers prefer? - Neither in particular. They want a clear design and working classes. Use whichever gets you there while communicating well.
Do I need to know formal UML notation? - No. A simple box and arrow sketch is enough. Precise symbols are not the point, clear communication is.
What if I run low on time? - Favour writing the core classes over perfecting a diagram. A working design beats a drawing every time.
Can I switch approaches midway? - Yes. Many people sketch a little, then drop into code once the shape is clear. That hybrid is often the strongest choice.
16. Key Takeaways

["UML first draws the structure before coding, code first lets it emerge.","UML first suits complex, many class problems, code first suits small focused ones.","You do not need formal UML, a rough box and arrow sketch is enough.","The hybrid, a quick sketch then code, is what most strong candidates use.","Whatever you choose, communicate and leave time to write real classes."]
items: UML first draws the structure before coding, code first lets it emerge.
UML first suits complex, many class problems, code first suits small focused ones.
You do not need formal UML, a rough box and arrow sketch is enough.
The hybrid, a quick sketch then code, is what most strong candidates use.
Whatever you choose, communicate and leave time to write real classes.

blocks.content: However you present it, the design will not survive first contact unchanged. Interviewers will push with follow up questions, and handling those well is the final piece.
